message.content: The hedgehog was the only thing in the world that had weight. His name was Dot, though he had never spoken it aloud, and his glasses were wire-rimmed, slightly bent on the left lens, and smelled faintly of the metallic tang of a world that no longer existed. He walked through a landscape that breathed in colors—not the colors of things, but colors as pure, unattached ideas. A field of cerulean swirled beside him, not reflecting light, not describing anything, simply *being* cerulean the way a thought is a thought. The ground beneath his quills was a flat plane of impasto ochre, thick and ridged like dried paint on a canvas. Above, the sky was a composition of intersecting arcs in vermillion and charcoal, neither rising nor falling, just *arranged*. Dot adjusted his glasses. The wire caught on a protrusion of magenta that grew from the ground like a frozen scream. His quills—each one individually keratin, each one a tiny calcium needle—pressed against the abstract surface and left a mark. A real mark. One with depth. One that could be scraped away. Reality was a foreign language in a country that had forgotten grammar. He found a puddle that morning—or what should have been a puddle. It was a perfect circle of cobalt, perfectly flat, with no meniscus, no reflection, no wetness. He leaned close. His glasses fogged slightly from his own body heat. In the fog, he saw his own nose: pink, moist, alive. When the fog cleared, the cobalt circle stared back at him with the indifferent patience of a Rothko. "Hello," he said to it. The cobalt did not respond. It did not need to. It was not a thing that *responded*. It was a shape that *was*. Dot sat down. His spine curved in a way that defied the geometry around him—there were no curves in this world that weren't deliberate, weren't part of a composition. His curve was accidental, biological, a function of intervertebral discs and the slow pull of a gravity that only he experienced. The ground beneath him darkened slightly where he sat. Not a color change. A *compression*. A real, physical indentation. He was, he realized, the only thing in the world that could change another thing. To be alive here was to be a mistake that kept insisting it was not one. Days passed, though "days" was generous. Time moved in the abstract world like pigment in water—slow, directionless, blooming outward without purpose. Dot walked for what felt like weeks. He found a mountain that was really just a triangle of burnt sienna, its edges so sharp they should have cut, but didn't, because they weren't edges—they were *boundaries*. He found a river that was a ribbon of gold leaf, flowing in a pattern that repeated every four inches, perfectly, forever, a loop without beginning or end. He drank from it. The water had no taste. Not "no taste" like water from a tap in a quiet house—no, it had *no quality of taste at all*, as if the concept had been surgically removed from the experience. It was liquid that was not wet. It was flow that was not motion. Dot set his water bowl—a real one, ceramic, chipped at the rim, found at the base of the sienna triangle—and drank from that instead. Loneliness, in an abstract world, was not the absence of others but the absence of anything that could miss you. He built a nest. It was a small pile of what passed for sticks—elongated slivers of cadmium yellow, rigid, flat, without grain or bark or the smell of decay. He arranged them around himself in a circle. His breathing fogged the air. His heart beat. These two facts—the fog, the beat—were the most revolutionary things in the world. At night (or what the world designated as night, a slow drift of the composition into deeper, cooler tones), Dot removed his glasses. Without them, the world became a smear. The colors bled into one another. The shapes lost their edges. And in that blur, for the first time, the world looked almost like something alive. Almost like a dream. Almost like the thing that had come before, the thing that had depth and weight and the ability to surprise itself. He put his glasses back on. The world snapped into its clean, composed indifference. But his nose was still pink. His quills still caught the light in tiny, individual glints. And the dent he had made in the ochre ground that morning was still there, a small dimple in the canvas of everything, a place where the real had pressed its thumb into the surface of the unreal and left a mark that nothing, in all its infinite, purposeless beauty, could paint over.
